title: A Conspiracy Of Credit Master Class: Part 2
summary: Eisman introduces bond contracts, yields, duration, taxation, ratings, credit analysis and amortization while warning about private-credit leverage and insurer connections. Several basic relationships are useful, but two central teaching claims fail: the five-year bond example confuses current yield with yield to maturity, and ratings do not mechanically set bond prices or equalize all same-rated yields. His four-C framework and acknowledgement of investors anticipating downgrades restore some missing judgment. Private-credit opacity has official support, while the scale and timing of eventual losses remain unresolved.
assessment: The lecture contains a material mathematical error and an overstated ratings-driven pricing model, rather than merely harmless terminology slips. The correct inverse price-yield relationship survives the incorrect numerical example. Distinguish conditional systemic-risk concerns from completed forecasts and unregulated from less prudentially regulated.
speaker_map_notes: This is a solo Steve Eisman lecture, established by self-identification at the opening. Brief SPEAKER_00 fragments within sentences are diarization errors, not a guest; the closing disclaimer is separate narration and not claim evidence.
framework_points: Read debt contracts and cash-flow timing before relying on labels.
Separate coupon, current yield and yield to maturity.
Treat ratings as one credit opinion rather than a price algorithm.
Trace leverage through portfolio companies, funds and insurers.
Assess capacity, collateral, covenants and character.
Distinguish maturity from duration and promised from realized return.
tools_and_charts: Treasury yield curve and high-grade/high-yield comparisons
transcript_cautions: Solo lecture has occasional SPEAKER_00 fragments that continue the same sentence.
The $1,250 example is coherent spoken arithmetic but incorrect finite-bond valuation; it is not silently corrected as a caption error.
Duration is repeatedly used where the conventional yield-curve axis is maturity.
Risk-free Treasuries are explicitly an assumption for the lecture.
Later discussion of investors anticipating downgrades qualifies earlier mechanical price-setting rhetoric.

claims.claim: A five-year $1,000 bond with a 7% annual coupon pays $70 yearly and repays principal at the end if it is a bullet bond.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Check call, default and amortization terms.
claims.reason: The cash-flow arithmetic is valid under the stated structure and successful repayment.
claims.next_check: Check call, default and amortization terms.
claims.deductive_proof: 0.07 times 1,000 equals 70. Under a bullet contract, scheduled principal is zero before year five and 1,000 in year five.

proof.derivation: 0.07 times 1,000 equals 70. Under a bullet contract, scheduled principal is zero before year five and 1,000 in year five.

claims.claim: A conventional amortizing residential mortgage repays principal gradually alongside interest until the loan balance reaches zero.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Distinguish fully amortizing, interest-only and balloon loans.
claims.qualifications: He refers to the ordinary 30-year mortgage example.
claims.reason: This follows from the fully amortizing payment schedule; it is not a claim about every possible mortgage structure.
claims.next_check: Distinguish fully amortizing, interest-only and balloon loans.
claims.deductive_proof: Balance Bt=Bt-1*(1+r)-payment. A fully amortizing payment is chosen so BN=0 after N scheduled payments; each payment covers interest r*Bt-1 and reduces principal by the remainder.
